name: Tara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy paper towels, bin liners and cleaning chemicals for Brightway Supply, a distributor out on the Canal Street industrial estate. Most mornings I check the stock sheet, ring my regular suppliers and place the orders, and then I chase the ones that are late. I'm still learning the pricing side, even after six years, so my boss Mr Hartley checks my bigger orders. By the end of the day my feet and my patience are both gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the phone calls. I've dealt with Gordon at the tissue mill for years and he tells me when a price rise is coming before it's official. What wears me out is the new stock screen they put in last spring. Pauline (a colleague) and I still keep paper notes because we don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the new screens save a few minutes, and that's about it. To friends I'd say the hype was a lot of noise, like most things. I wouldn't post anything online, because I don't use that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still worried. Nothing big changes, but my pay is low, I've got no savings, and a firm like ours is always looking for a cheaper way to do reorders. Even a small change could touch my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep my notebook and keep ringing Gordon at the mill. I'd also stop the takeaway Fridays, which is about 40 a week, and put that aside in case the firm trims the buying desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat and a bit tiring. Nothing is falling apart, but I'm 58 and I've nothing behind me. I can't relax, because one bad quarter at Brightway and somebody has to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Dennis's wage covers the rent. What would happen to the household if your hours were cut by a day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Dennis works part-time at the garden centre. His wage covers the rent and mine covers everything else. If my hours were cut by even a day, we'd be skipping the electricity top-up, and that's what keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the firm would really use software to replace the buying desk, even without any big change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not scared of a computer. I'm scared of the boss saying a computer made the decision. Then there's no one to argue with. I used to be a union rep, so I know how that goes.

say: I'd say the **new screens** save a few minutes and nothing more.
I'd tell friends the **hype** was mostly noise, and I wouldn't post anything online.
think: I'm still worried, because my **pay is low** and there's no cushion behind me.
Even small changes could let the firm trim the **buying desk** I sit at.
I used to be a union rep, so I fear **nobody to argue** with.
do: **Keep** my notebook and my calls to Gordon at the tissue mill exactly as they are.
**Stop** the 40-a-week Friday takeaway and put the money aside.
Watch what the firm does at the next **quarter** before I decide anything.
feel: **Flat** and tired, because nothing is falling apart but nothing is secure either.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of a computer. I'm scared of the boss saying a computer made the decision. Then there's no one to argue with.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money**, not technology: a thin cushion and low pay make even a mild picture feel risky.
**Union** past shows up strongly; she frames AI as a way for bosses to avoid accountability.
She sounded composed but named a clear route to hardship (one lost day of hours).

steps.text: Keep ringing Gordon at the tissue mill and writing orders in my notebook
Drop the 40-a-week Friday takeaway and set the money aside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd keep my head down and say it's early days. To friends I'd say it's the bosses using AI to cut wages again. Reordering is exactly what they'd give to software first, and I'd say that out loud to anybody who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my desk goes. Brightway only needs one person to watch the screen, and Pauline is younger and learns faster than I do. I never use AI, I don't trust it, and I haven't tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to the union we had at my old warehouse and ask them to speak up for the buyers here. I'd also open a savings pot with 50 a week, even if it hurts. And I'd write to our local councillor about older workers being dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair and a bit frightening. I've worked since I was seventeen. I don't want to be pushed out into a job market with hardly any buying jobs nearby, at an age when nobody wants to take someone on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Elena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Elena that I might be out of work before 62, and that she shouldn't be surprised if I need a bit of help with bills. I hate saying it. But I'd rather she hears it from me than finds out when the rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the new system if your boss asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hartley asked me to learn the new system, I'd try, but I'd want it in writing that my job isn't the price of that training. I've seen people train their replacement before, and I won't do it.

say: I'd say it's **early days** at work, and bosses are using AI to **cut wages** again.
I'd tell anyone listening that reordering is exactly what firms hand to software first.
think: I think my **desk goes**, because Pauline is younger and learns faster than me.
I never use AI and don't trust it, so I'm starting from **behind**.
do: **Contact** the union from my old warehouse and ask them to speak for the buyers.
**Open** a savings pot with 50 a week from now.
**Write** to my councillor about older workers being dropped.
feel: **Unfair** and frightening, after working since I was seventeen.
S1.quote: I don't want to be pushed out into a job market with hardly any buying jobs nearby, at an age when nobody wants to take someone on.
fieldNote: She expects her own **desk** to go and says so plainly, so alarmed fits despite her steady tone.
Her instinct is collective: union, councillor, family, not retraining by herself.
Refuses to train her own replacement; a trust issue more than a skills one.

steps.text: Contact the old warehouse union about speaking for the buyers at Brightway
Put 50 a week into a separate savings pot
Write to the councillor about older workers being dropped

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody asked us. At work I'd keep quiet, but with friends I'd say governments must step in before ordinary people are left with nothing. We're not ready, and the firms know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think that's it for me. Buying is thinking work, and two years isn't long enough to learn anything new at 58. I'd be done by 2028 with no pension worth the name, and I can't see where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go to the union and the council the same week, though I'm not sure they'd have an answer. I'd cancel the car insurance extras and stop buying anything but food. And I'd ask the pension people what happens if I take it at 60 instead of 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing in front of a train. I can't think straight about it. I know I should have a plan, but a plan costs money and time, and I have neither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to first, and what would you ask them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Marco is in the shipping office at the port. If the firm lays me off, I'd ask whether he can put a word in for me, though I know they're cutting too. I'd be embarrassed to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to name one bill that goes unpaid first, which would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hardest part is that nobody would know what to do either. I wouldn't expect the government to have a plan. If I'm honest, I'd just keep going to Brightway each day until somebody told me not to.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and governments must step in before ordinary people are left with nothing.
At work I'd stay quiet, but with friends I'd say the firms **know** we're not ready.
think: I think that's **it for me**, because buying is thinking work and two years isn't long enough to relearn.
I'd have **no pension** worth the name and nowhere obvious to go.
do: **Go** to the union and the council in the same week, though I doubt they'd have answers.
**Cancel** the insurance extras and buy only food.
**Ask** the pension people what happens if I draw it at 60.
feel: Like standing in front of a **train**, unable to think straight.
Ashamed that I'd have **no plan**, because a plan costs money and time.
S2.quote: I know I should have a plan, but a plan costs money and time, and I have neither.
fieldNote: **Panicked** is deliberate: no savings, no local jobs, no appetite for new tools, and a two-year clock.
She looks first to institutions, then to her son, and is embarrassed by both.
Practical in small ways, such as the pension question, but cannot see a route.

steps.text: Visit the union and the council in the same week
Cancel the car insurance extras and buy only food
Ask the pension office what happens if I draw it at 60
Ask my son Marco at the port whether his office has any openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's long enough to be organised. At work I'd tell Mr Hartley that the buyers should hear the plan first, not read it in an email. With friends I'd say we need the unions in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd just about make it to my pension before it lands on me. By 2031 I'd be 63. The trouble is the gap between a job ending and a pension I can actually live on, and I've no money for that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by getting my savings to a month, then three. I'd talk to the union about a redundancy deal for the buying desk. And I'd think about going part-time at 62 if they'd let me, so I'd have a soft landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like I've got time but not enough of the things I need to use it, which is money. It's a bit like seeing a flood coming and having no sandbags.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What difference does having five years make for you compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Dennis would have to carry on at the garden centre as long as his knee lets him. We've talked about downsizing the flat. I'd rather keep it, but I'd sell up before I'd take on debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather keep the flat. What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years later doesn't help me, because my work is the thinking part. It might help Dennis's garden centre friends, but not the buying desk at Brightway.

say: I'd tell Mr Hartley the **buyers** should hear any plan first, not read it in an email.
I'd say with friends that **unions** need to be in the room.
think: I think I'd **just about** reach my pension before it lands, but the gap worries me.
I have no money to cover the **gap** between a job ending and a liveable pension.
do: **Raise** my savings to one month of bills, then three.
**Ask** the union for a redundancy deal covering the buying desk.
**Request** part-time hours from 62 for a softer landing.
feel: Like seeing a **flood** coming with no sandbags.
Grateful for the time, but short of the **money** to use it.
S3.quote: I've got time but not enough of the things I need to use it, which is money.
fieldNote: Extra time helps her plan, but **cash** is the missing ingredient, so she stays at alarmed.
Names the pension gap precisely; this is where her mind goes first.
Robots arriving later mean nothing to her because her tasks are all desk work.

steps.text: Raise my savings to one month of bills, then three
Ask the union for a redundancy deal covering the buying desk
Request part-time hours from 62 for a softer landing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and I'd mean it for the younger ones. I'm 58, so by 2036 I'll be nearly 68 and long retired. With friends I'd say the young ones need to be taught properly, not just told to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel less scared for me, but still worried about money. The pension's the issue. If prices go up and the state pension doesn't, I'd still be counting every penny at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save as hard as I can for the next seven years, aiming at a proper cushion. I'd stay in the union and push for training for the young ones. And I'd see whether Elena wants to learn something that can't be done by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels almost calm, but with a sore patch. I'm glad the worst of it falls mostly after my time, yet I'd feel sad for my daughter's generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything different to your daughter Elena than to people at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena works in a call centre, which is probably the first thing to go. If ten years is true, I'd tell her to move now into something with her hands, like care work or an electrician's apprenticeship. I'd gladly help with the fees if I'd saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you if the pension doesn't keep up with prices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The real difference with ten years is that I'd have a chance. In the fast one I'd have nothing. Here, if I keep my head down and save, I could retire before it reaches Brightway properly.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** of time, and the young ones should be taught properly.
I'd tell friends that **training** matters more than being told to adapt.
think: I'd feel less scared for me, since I'd be **68** and long retired by 2036.
I'd still worry the **pension** won't keep up with prices.
do: **Save** hard for seven years and aim for a proper cushion.
**Stay** in the union and push for training for the young.
**Help** my daughter Elena into care work or an apprenticeship.
feel: **Almost calm** for myself, but sad for my daughter's generation.
S4.quote: In the fast one I'd have nothing. Here, if I keep my head down and save, I could retire before it reaches Brightway properly.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her relax about her own job but not her **money**; anxious fits the pension worry.
Her concern moves to her daughter, whose call-centre job is exposed.
The contrast with the two-year picture is spelled out without prompting.

steps.text: Save hard for seven years towards a cushion of several months
Stay in the union and push for training for younger staff
Offer to help Elena with fees for an apprenticeship or care course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. I'm 58, there's no savings to speak of, and there are hardly any other buying jobs round here. If it went that fast I'd be out before my pension is anywhere near enough, and nobody would have a plan ready.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get told to retrain at 58 as if that's simple. Nobody asks who pays the rent while we do it. I'd like someone to ask the bosses that question out loud.

headlineQuote: I'd be out before my pension is anywhere near enough, and nobody would have a plan ready.
portrait: Tara is 58, a junior buyer at **Brightway Supply**, with a partner, two grown children and almost no savings.
She is **resistant** to new tools and never uses AI, so every scenario feels like something done to her.
Her **union** past shapes how she reads change: she blames bosses and looks to groups, councillors and family for help.
She grows more frightened as the date comes closer, and she is **panicked** if AGI arrives within two years.
Her main fear is the **gap** between losing her desk and living on a pension she can't yet afford.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because she has no savings, few nearby jobs and no time to learn new skills.
whatWouldHelp: Someone to tell **bosses** to pay for training, and a bridge payment until her pension starts.
